sections.title: Three verb forms: now, command, dictionary
body: A verb is a doing word. Today you need three verb forms. The present tense says what happens now or regularly. It ends in r: talar, köper, bor. The help verbs kan, vill, ska and måste are the exceptions, and so is vet (know) on page 8: Jag vet inte. Swedish uses one form for I study and I am studying: Jag pluggar. English (I am studying) and Hindi (मैं पढ़ रहा हूँ, main padh rahā hūn) both add am. Swedish never does, so Jag är pluggar is wrong.

The imperative (command form) tells someone to do something: Tala! Köp! Ring! Your teacher calls it the naked verb. Later tenses are built on it, so it is worth learning well. The infinitive is the dictionary form. It follows a help verb and usually ends in a: tala, köpa, ringa. Dictionaries often show it with att (to): att tala = to speak.

Make the forms from the present tense, in three groups. Ar verbs: take away r. Talar becomes Tala! and tala; the command and the infinitive look the same. Er verbs: take away er for the command, then add a for the infinitive. Köper becomes Köp! and köpa. Short verbs: take away r. Bor becomes Bo! and bo; this infinitive does not end in a (also må).

Two verbs need extra care. Vara (be) is irregular: är in the present and Var! as a command. Kommer keeps only one m in the command: Kom! The infinitive is komma. The o in Kom! stays short, as in kommer: Swedish never writes mm at the end of a word. So Kom hem! has two short vowels (remember long and short from Lecture 1).

examples.fi: Jag talar svenska. · Tala svenska! · Jag kan tala svenska.
examples.en: I speak Swedish. · Speak Swedish! · I can speak Swedish.
examples.note: Ar verb: present, command, infinitive.

examples.fi: Jag köper bröd. · Köp bröd! · Jag vill köpa bröd.
examples.en: I buy bread. · Buy bread! · I want to buy bread.
examples.note: Er verb: köper loses er for the command (Köp!), then adds a for the infinitive (köpa).

examples.fi: Jag mår bra. · Må bra! · Jag vill må bättre.
examples.en: I feel well. · Be well! · I want to feel better.
examples.note: Short verb: mår loses r. The infinitive må does not end in a.

examples.en: He is coming home. · Come home! · He has to come home.
examples.note: Kommer keeps only one m in the command: Kom!

examples.en: I am happy. · Be happy! · I want to be happy.

activity.label: Sort verb forms
activity.title: Which job does this verb form do?
activity.instructions: Look only at the Swedish: an r ending, a help verb before it, or no subject at all. Is the marked verb the present, a command, or the infinitive?

items.why: Talar ends in r: it says what she does. Hon talar svenska = She speaks Swedish.
No r, no subject, no help verb: it tells someone to act. Tala långsamt! = Speak slowly!
It follows the help verb kan, so it is the infinitive. Jag kan tala svenska = I can speak Swedish.
Köper ends in r: present tense. Jag köper bröd = I buy bread.
Köper loses er: Köp! is the command. Köp bröd! = Buy bread!
After vill, the verb ends in a: köpa. Jag vill köpa bröd = I want to buy bread.
Ringer loses er: Ring! is the command. Ring mig! = Call me!
After måste, use the infinitive ringa. Hon måste ringa nu = She must call now.
Var! is the command of vara (be). Var glad! = Be happy!

activity.summary: Ask what the verb is doing: telling what happens (present, r), giving an instruction (command), or following a help verb (infinitive).

sections.title: Help verbs open the door to an infinitive
body: Kan (can), vill (want to), måste (must, have to) and ska (will, be going to) are help verbs. The verb after them is the infinitive, with no att: kan tala, vill köpa, måste jobba, ska träna. Not kan talar, and not vill att köpa, even though English says want to. On page 8, Jag vill inte att du blir sen has att only because a new person (du) does the second action.
Careful with vill. It looks like English will, but it means want to. For a plan (will, going to), use ska: I morgon ska jag träna.
Hinner (have time to) and orkar (have the energy to) work the same way: Jag hinner gå till affären. Jag orkar inte plugga. After these two, att is possible but never needed.

Two useful questions. Kan du …? asks for help politely: Kan du hjälpa mig? Ska vi …? suggests a plan: Ska vi dricka kaffe? To want a thing, say vill ha: Jag vill ha kaffe, not Jag vill kaffe. In a café, order with tack: En kaffe, tack. Snälla at the start of a sentence sounds like begging.

Careful: English must not is not måste inte in Swedish. A ban is får inte: Du får inte röka här (You must not smoke here). No need is behöver inte: Du behöver inte komma (You don’t have to come). Lecture 13 practises both.

examples.fi: Jag kan sjunga, men jag kan inte dansa.
examples.en: I can sing, but I cannot dance.
examples.note: Both verbs after kan are infinitives.

examples.fi: Jag vill ha kaffe.
examples.en: I want coffee.
examples.note: Use vill ha for wanting a thing.

examples.fi: I morgon ska jag träffa Elin.
examples.en: Tomorrow I’m going to meet Elin.
examples.note: Ska marks a plan; träffa is the infinitive.

examples.fi: Jag måste ringa hälsostationen.
examples.en: I have to call the health centre.
examples.note: In Helsinki the public health centre is called hälsostation in Swedish (in Sweden: vårdcentral).

examples.fi: Jag hinner gå till affären.
examples.en: I have time to go to the shop.
examples.note: Hinner is about time.

examples.fi: Kan du hjälpa mig?
examples.en: Can you help me?
examples.note: Kan du …? is a polite request.

examples.fi: Ska vi dricka kaffe?
examples.en: Shall we have coffee?
examples.note: Ska vi …? suggests a plan.

activity.pattern: Help verb + infinitive: kan simma, vill sova, måste jobba, ska träna.

sections.title: Inte comes after the first verb
body: Inte means not. It makes a sentence negative. Put inte straight after the first verb. One verb: Jag simmar inte. With a help verb: Jag kan inte simma. Kan is the first verb, so inte comes before the infinitive simma.

English adds do: I do not swim. Swedish never adds an extra verb. The rule works with every help verb: Jag vill inte ha kaffe. Jag hinner inte komma. In a command, inte also follows the verb: Läs inte mer! Oroa dig inte!

If you think in Hindi, watch out. Hindi puts नहीं before the verb (मैं नहीं जाता, main nahīn jātā = I don’t go), so Jag inte går may feel right. Swedish wants Jag går inte. Marathi puts नाही after the verb (मी जात नाही, mī jāt nāhī), which is closer to Swedish. But Marathi नाही ends the sentence, and Swedish inte does not: Jag talar inte finska, not Jag talar finska inte.
Short adverbs such as ofta (often), alltid (always) and aldrig (never) go in the same place as inte: Jag dricker ofta kaffe. Jag dricker aldrig vin.
Finland-Swedish note: in fast speech in Helsinki you will often hear int instead of inte. Recognise it, but write inte.

examples.fi: Jag gillar choklad. → Jag gillar inte choklad.
examples.en: I like chocolate. → I do not like chocolate.
examples.note: After the only verb.

examples.fi: Jag kan inte komma i kväll.
examples.en: I cannot come tonight.
examples.note: After kan, before komma.

examples.fi: Jag vill inte ha kaffe.
examples.en: I do not want coffee.
examples.note: After vill, before ha.

examples.fi: I kväll orkar jag inte laga mat.
examples.en: Tonight I don’t have the energy to cook.
examples.note: Time first: verb, then jag, then inte.

examples.fi: Jag talar inte finska, men jag talar lite svenska.
examples.en: I don’t speak Finnish, but I speak a little Swedish.
examples.note: From Lecture 1 (Jag talar …): talar is the only verb, so inte follows it. A line you will use in Helsinki.

examples.fi: Oroa dig inte!
examples.en: Don’t worry!
examples.note: In a command, inte follows the verb and dig.

sections.memoryTip: Find the first verb. Park inte directly after it.
sections.tryIt: Make these negative aloud: Jag jobbar. Jag kan dansa. Jag ska träna. (Check: Jag jobbar inte. Jag kan inte dansa. Jag ska inte träna.)

activity.label: Place inte
activity.title: Which word order is correct?
activity.instructions: Sort each sentence: is inte (or ofta, aldrig) after the first verb?

buckets.label: Correct
buckets.hint: inte or aldrig after the first verb

items.why: Inte follows kan.
Move inte after kan: Jag kan inte sjunga.
Inte follows dricker.
Say Vi ska inte äta pizza.
Jobbar is the first verb. Jag comes right after it, then inte.

items.en: I don’t have the energy to study.
items.why: Say Jag orkar inte plugga.
Aldrig sits where inte would be: after dricker.
Say Jag dricker aldrig vin.

activity.summary: First verb, then inte: kan inte, vill inte, jobbar inte. Ofta, alltid and aldrig go in the same place.

sections.title: The verb stays second
body: The golden rule of Swedish word order is verb second (V2): in a statement, the first verb is always the second building block. Position one can be the person (Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag), a time (I dag bakar min mamma en kaka) or a place (I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe).

The subject always stands right next to the verb: just before it or just after it. When a time or a place comes first, the subject moves to just after the verb. Count chunks, not words: I dag is one chunk in position one.

With a help verb and inte: I morgon ska jag inte jobba. Ska is in position two, then jag, then inte, then the infinitive (verb 2) in its own slot. Questions with a question word follow the same rule: Varför kommer du sent?

Two common slips. English says Today I work, so learners say I dag jag jobbar. Swedish needs I dag jobbar jag. Hindi and Marathi put the verb near the end, so check that the verb has not drifted to the end. Learners of Swedish often master this swap late, so say time-first lines aloud many times.

examples.fi: Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag.
examples.en: My mother is baking a cake today.
examples.note: Subject first, verb second.

examples.fi: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.
examples.en: Today my mother is baking a cake.
examples.note: Time first, then the verb, then the subject.

examples.fi: Tyvärr kan jag inte komma i kväll.
examples.en: Unfortunately I can’t come tonight.
examples.note: Tyvärr (unfortunately) is position one, so kan comes next. Later in the sentence it goes where inte goes: Jag kan tyvärr inte komma.

examples.fi: I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe varje dag.
examples.en: In Finland we drink a lot of coffee every day.
examples.note: Place first, dricker second.

examples.fi: Varför kommer du sent?
examples.en: Why are you late?
examples.note: The question word is position one; kommer is position two.

sections.memoryTip: Start with who, when or where. Then the verb must arrive immediately.
sections.tryIt: Change Jag jobbar i dag to start with I dag. Then change Jag ska inte träna i morgon to start with I morgon. (Check: I dag jobbar jag. I morgon ska jag inte träna.)

activity.label: Verb-second check
activity.title: Does the verb hold position two?
activity.instructions: Count the opening chunk as position one. Sort each line.

items.fi: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.
items.en: Today my mother is baking a cake.
items.why: I dag is first; bakar is second.

items.fi: I dag min mamma bakar en kaka.
items.en: Today my mother is baking a cake.
items.why: Say I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.

items.fi: Just nu kan jag inte plugga.
items.why: Kan is in position two.

items.en: Tomorrow I am going to exercise.
items.why: Say I morgon ska jag träna.

items.fi: I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe.
items.en: In Finland we drink a lot of coffee.
items.why: I Finland is one chunk; dricker is second.
Say Varje dag dricker jag kaffe.
Subject first, verb second. The time can also go at the end.

activity.summary: Time first causes the swap: I dag + verb + subject.

guided.hint: After kan, use the dictionary form.
guided.explanation: Kan tala: after a help verb, use the infinitive, without att (English to does not carry over).

guided.prompt: Alex says: “Jag är så trött!” Choose the right verb (sover, köper, ringer), then type its command form: ___ nu!
guided.hint: A tired person needs sleep. Sover is an er verb: take away er.
guided.explanation: Sov nu! Sover loses er: Sov! Elin says the same thing in the story.

guided.prompt: Choose the correct Swedish for “I am studying.”
guided.hint: Swedish present covers both study and am studying.
guided.explanation: Jag pluggar. English I am studying and Hindi पढ़ रहा हूँ both have am; Swedish has no am here.

guided.prompt: There is no help verb here. Elin ___ kaffe varje morgon.
guided.hint: Without kan, vill, måste or ska, use the present tense.
guided.explanation: Elin dricker kaffe varje morgon. With no help verb, the verb is in the present (r). Compare: Elin vill dricka kaffe.

guided.prompt: Alex’s test is tomorrow. He says: “I have to study tonight.” Jag ___ plugga i kväll.
guided.hint: Have to is a need, not a wish or an ability.
guided.explanation: Jag måste plugga i kväll. Måste = must, have to.

guided.prompt: Make a softer request: “Can you speak slowly, please?” ___ du tala långsamt, snälla?
guided.hint: Ask about ability to make it polite.
guided.explanation: Kan du …? is a polite request. Måste du …? means Do you have to …?

guided.prompt: Make it negative and type the whole sentence: Jag orkar plugga. (I have the energy to study.)
guided.hint: Find the first verb, then put inte right after it.
guided.explanation: Jag orkar inte plugga: inte comes right after orkar, the first verb.

guided.prompt: Lecture 1 line: Jag bor i Finland nu. Start it with Nu (now) and type the whole sentence.
guided.hint: Nu first, then the verb, then jag.
guided.explanation: Nu bor jag i Finland. From Lecture 1: Nu takes position one, so bor stays second and jag moves after it, just like I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.

guided.prompt: A mother phones her son and says: “Come home!” Type the command of kommer with hem (home).
guided.hint: Kommer loses er, and mm becomes one m. Hem means home (page 7: När kommer du hem?).
guided.explanation: Kom hem! Kommer → Kom!, with one m.

missionPlan.title: Plan six short lines
missionPlan.intro: Elin asks: Vad kan du göra? Vad vill du göra? Vad måste du göra? Vad hinner du inte göra i veckan? Plan one line for each answer, and three for kan.

words.translation: I don’t have the energy to read.

words.example: Jag har ett prov i morgon.

words.translation: I want to pass the test.

words.en: please (at the end of a request)

words.example: Tyvärr kan jag inte i kväll.

pronunciation.text: Jag kan tala. Kan du komma? Kom hem! Jag måste sova. Sov nu! Oroa dig inte!
pronunciation.tip: Long or short, as in Lecture 1. Kan has a short a (one n, like han and men), but tala has a long a. Kom! and hem are short too: Swedish never ends a word with mm. Sova and Sov! sound like ‘såva’ and ‘såv’. The app’s Sweden-Swedish voices sing two-syllable words such as tala and sova with a two-peaked melody. Finland-Swedish has no such melody, so you do not need it: just stress the first syllable. Say mig and dig like mej and dej.

reading_passage.text:
Hej Alex!
I dag har du provet. Oroa dig inte! Ät frukost och drick vatten. Läs inte mer nu. Lycka till! Ring mig efter provet.
Hälsningar, Elin

options: To wish Alex luck and give advice before his test.
To invite Alex to a party.
To say that she is ill.
gist.explanation: I dag har du provet … Lycka till! She writes on the morning of his test.

detail.prompt: What should Alex not do now?
detail.explanation: Läs inte mer nu: Don’t read any more now.

reading.text:
Hej Alex!
I dag har du provet. Oroa dig inte! Ät frukost och drick vatten. Läs inte mer nu. Lycka till! Ring mig efter provet.
Hälsningar, Elin
reading.question: When does Elin want Alex to call her?
reading.explanation: Ring mig efter provet: Call me after the test.

listening.text: I dag jobbar Elin hela dagen. Sedan måste hon laga mat. Hon vill träna, men hon hinner inte. I morgon ska hon inte jobba. Hon ska vila och träffa en vän.
listening.question: Why does Elin not exercise today?
listening.explanation: Hon vill träna, men hon hinner inte.

speaking.prompt: Elin asks about you and your week, the way a YKI examiner asks guide questions. Answer each in a full sentence: Vad kan du göra? (three things) · Vad vill du göra? · Vad måste du göra? · Vad hinner du inte göra i veckan?
speaking.help: Jag kan … · Jag vill … · Jag måste … / I morgon måste jag … · Jag hinner inte … i veckan.
speaking.model: Jag kan tala hindi och engelska. Jag kan laga mat. Jag kan simma. Jag vill träna. I morgon måste jag plugga svenska. Jag hinner inte simma i veckan.

writing.prompt: Write a short message: say sorry, say why you cannot meet tonight, and suggest what, where and when instead.
writing.situation: Your friend Elin writes: “Vi ses i kväll!” (See you tonight!) But you are tired and have a test tomorrow. Write back and cancel. This is a real YKI basic-level task type: a short message that cancels a plan.
points: Say sorry and say that you cannot meet tonight.
Say why: you are tired and must study.
Suggest another plan: what, where and when.
End with a greeting and your name.
writing.help: Hej Elin! · Förlåt! (Sorry!) · Tyvärr kan jag inte … (Unfortunately I can’t …: tyvärr first, then kan) · Jag är trött och måste plugga. · Vi kan dricka kaffe i centrum på fredag. (We can have coffee in the centre on Friday.) · Hinner du då? (Do you have time then?) · Hälsningar (Best wishes) and your name.
writing.model:
Hej Elin!
Förlåt! Tyvärr kan jag inte träffa dig i kväll. Jag är trött och måste plugga. I morgon har jag ett prov. Vi kan dricka kaffe i centrum på fredag. Hinner du då?
Hälsningar, Alex

route.expectedOutput: Answer Elin’s four questions about your week: three things you can do, one thing you want to do, one thing you must do, and one thing you have no time for. Then write a message: say sorry, say why you cannot meet tonight, and suggest what, where and when instead.
route.transferPrompt: Say the same plan again, but begin two lines with I dag or I morgon.
route.returnPrompt: From memory, say one kan line, one måste line and one negative line in under 20 seconds.
successChecks: Say six lines: three with kan, one with vill, one with måste and one with inte.
Use the infinitive after each help verb: kan tala, not kan talar.
Put inte after the first verb.

unplannedQuestions.sample: Nej, jag kan inte tala finska. Men jag kan tala lite svenska. / Ja, lite.

unplannedQuestions.fi: Vad måste du göra i dag?
unplannedQuestions.sample: Jag måste jobba. / I dag måste jag plugga.

unplannedQuestions.en: What do you want to drink?
unplannedQuestions.sample: Jag vill dricka kaffe. / Jag vill ha vatten, tack.

unplannedQuestions.fi: Vad ska du göra i morgon?
unplannedQuestions.en: What are you going to do tomorrow?
Do you have the energy to exercise tonight?
unplannedQuestions.sample: Nej, jag orkar inte. / Ja, jag orkar.

unplannedQuestions.fi: Kan du komma på kaffe i kväll?
unplannedQuestions.en: Can you come for coffee tonight?
unplannedQuestions.sample: Nej, jag kan inte i kväll. Jag måste plugga. Men jag hinner på fredag. / Ja, jag kan komma.

checkpoint.prompt: Start with I dag and write in Swedish: “Today I can’t study.”
answers: I dag kan jag inte plugga.
I dag kan jag inte studera.
checkpoint.hint: Time first, then the first verb, then jag, then inte.
checkpoint.explanation: I dag kan jag inte plugga: the verb kan stays in position two.

checkpoint.prompt: In a shop in Helsinki someone speaks Finnish to you. Which is correct?
checkpoint.hint: Talar (Lecture 1) is the only verb. Put inte right after it.
checkpoint.explanation: Jag talar inte finska. From Lecture 1: talar is the first verb, so inte comes straight after it. Not before the verb (the Hindi order) and not at the very end (where Marathi puts नाही).

checkpoint.prompt: Fix the one mistake and type the sentence (keep vill): Jag vill läser mer.
checkpoint.hint: After vill, use the infinitive. Läser is an er verb.
checkpoint.explanation: Jag vill läsa mer. Take away er, then add a: läser → läsa (not läse).

checkpoint.prompt: What does Jag hinner inte komma mean?
answers: I don’t have time to come.
options: I don’t have time to come.
I don’t have the energy to come.
checkpoint.explanation: Hinner = have time. Orkar = have the energy. Vill = want.

checkpoint.prompt: Write the command form of ringer: “___ mig i morgon!” (Call me tomorrow!)
checkpoint.explanation: Ring mig i morgon! The command is the naked verb: ringer → Ring!

checkpoint.prompt: Elin writes: “Jag kan inte komma i kväll.” Ask her why, with varför from Lecture 2: “Why can’t you come?”
answers: Varför kan du inte komma i kväll?
Varför kan du inte komma ikväll?
Varför kan inte du komma i kväll?
Varför kan inte du komma ikväll?
checkpoint.hint: Varför is position one. Then the first verb, then du, then inte, then the infinitive.
checkpoint.explanation: Varför kan du inte komma? The question word from Lecture 2 takes position one, kan stays second, and inte comes after du, as in Varför kommer du sent?

assignment.title: Episode 3 mission: My week
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Answer Vad kan du göra? (three things), Vad vill du göra?, Vad måste du göra? and Vad hinner du inte göra i veckan?

CHANGE: Start two lines with I dag or I morgon and keep the verb second.

RETURN: Tomorrow, say a kan line, a måste line and a negative line without looking.
assignment.model: Jag kan tala hindi och engelska. Jag kan laga mat. Jag kan simma. Jag vill träna. I morgon måste jag plugga svenska. Jag hinner inte simma i veckan.

takeaways: Present tense usually ends in r; the command is the naked verb; the infinitive is the dictionary form that follows a help verb.
After kan, vill, måste and ska, use the infinitive with no att: Jag kan tala. Jag vill sova.
Put inte after the first verb: Jag kan inte komma. In a command too: Oroa dig inte!
A time phrase may come first, but the verb stays second: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.
